source: Dewey (1910) How We Think, ch. 1
finding: Dewey defines reflective thinking as careful testing of a belief against its grounds. Two sub-processes sit under every act of it: a felt doubt and a search for facts.
numbers: Two sub-processes: (1) perplexity, hesitation, doubt; (2) an act of search or investigation.
quote: Active, persistent, and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it.
limits: Philosophical analysis from examples, no experiment. No data on how often people think this way.
agent_relevance: The two-part shape (doubt, then search for facts that confirm or nullify) matches a verify-before-commit loop. Background only.

source: Dewey (1910) How We Think, ch. 6 (p. 72)
finding: Dewey lists five logically distinct steps in a complete act of reflection. Steps 1 and 2 often fuse. Later he called them phases, not a fixed order.
numbers: Five steps: felt difficulty; location and definition; suggestion of a solution; reasoning out its bearings; further observation and experiment leading to acceptance or rejection.
limits: Built from three everyday cases, not tested. Dewey (1933) dropped the idea of a fixed sequence.
agent_relevance: Direct ancestor of define, hypothesise, reason, test loops. Our states S0-S9 already cover this; nothing new to add.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Hitchcock) Critical Thinking: Dewey section
finding: The entry restates Dewey and notes his 1933 revision from steps to phases to remove the implication of fixed order.
numbers: Quote cited as Dewey 1910:6, 1933:9. Entry counts 11 paradigm examples.
limits: Secondary source.
agent_relevance: Confirms the loop is non-linear; our program, not the model, should own transitions.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia (Hitchcock): history and Ennis definitions
finding: Ennis proposed 12 aspects of critical thinking in 1962. He later gave a streamlined conception (1991) using 'reasonable' as the norm and added care for persons (1996). By 2016 he listed 17 definitions (14 scholarly, 3 dictionary) as conceptions of one concept.
numbers: 12 aspects (1962); 17 definitions (2016); combining ability lists gives more than 50 possible objectives.
limits: The visible page text did not quote the Ennis 1962 or 1987 definitions.
agent_relevance: No single agreed definition exists, so any CT score for an agent depends on which definition is picked. Pick one and state it.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report executive summary: method
finding: APA-commissioned Delphi study: 46 experts, six rounds from Feb 1988 to Nov 1989, anonymised synthesis by one director. Panel was 52% philosophy, 22% education, 20% social science, 6% physical science. One expert asked to be excluded from the findings.
numbers: N=46 panelists; 6 rounds (R1 11 Feb 1988 to R6 25 Sep 1989); working assumption: CT can be assessed validly and reliably.
limits: Expert opinion, not data on thinking. Philosophy-heavy panel. Aimed at freshman and sophomore college level.
agent_relevance: Definitions of CT are a consensus of philosophers, not measured outcomes. Use as a specification language, not evidence of effect.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report: consensus statement
finding: Consensus definition: CT is purposeful, self-regulatory judgment yielding interpretation, analysis, evaluation and inference plus explanation of the grounds. It is 'pervasive and self-rectifying' and not synonymous with good thinking.
numbers: One paragraph (Table 1) with 14 traits of the ideal critical thinker.
quote: purposeful, self-regulatory judgment which results in interpretation, analysis, evaluation, and inference
limits: Consensus of the panel; a minority dissent on parts (see a09).
agent_relevance: The definition already holds self-regulation and explanation of grounds, which map to our checking and written-justification guardrails.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report: six core skills and sub-skills
finding: Six core skills with 16 sub-skills: interpretation (categorization, decoding significance, clarifying meaning); analysis (examining ideas, detecting arguments, analyzing arguments); evaluation (assessing claims, assessing arguments); inference (querying evidence, conjecturing alternatives, drawing conclusions); explanation (stating results, justifying procedures, presenting arguments); self-regulation (self-examination, self-correction).
numbers: Agreement: analysis, evaluation, inference over 95% central; interpretation, explanation, self-regulation over 87%.
limits: Consensus covers the descriptions, not the examples.
agent_relevance: Usable as a checklist of operations. Conjecturing alternatives and self-correction map to our operators and verification; interpretation maps to restating the problem.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report: dispositions (Table 5)
finding: 19 dispositions: 12 'approaches to life' (inquisitiveness, staying informed, alertness, trust in reasoned inquiry, self-confidence in reasoning, open-mindedness, flexibility, understanding others, fair-mindedness, honesty about bias, prudence in judgment, willingness to reconsider) and 7 'approaches to specific issues' (clarity, orderliness, diligence, reasonable criteria, care in focus, persistence, precision).
numbers: 19 dispositions (12 plus 7). 83% agree good thinkers show them.
limits: Human attitudes cannot be implemented directly; only behavioural counterparts (persistence, diligence in seeking information) can be coded as rules.
agent_relevance: Dispositions suggest budget and retry rules (persistence, diligence in search), not model 'attitude'.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report: dispute over dispositions in the meaning of CT
finding: The panel split: 61% held affective dispositions are part of the meaning of CT; about 30% held CT is a procedural skill set only and a skilled sophist is still a critical thinker. All agreed on using dispositions to describe the paradigm good thinker.
numbers: 61% inclusive view; about 30% strict procedural view; 83% consensus on the paradigm list. Finding: denying CT because one disapproves ethically is improper.
limits: Percentages from the report text; with 46 panelists 61% is about 28 people.
agent_relevance: For an agent only the procedural view is implementable: define quality by procedure (checks done), not character.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report: domain knowledge and assessment
finding: Experts say CT skills transcend subjects but using them needs domain knowledge. CT is one of several higher-order forms (problem solving, decision making, creative thinking). They state that correlations between other tasks and CT sub-skills had not been established. 15 recommendations include using several assessment methods.
numbers: 15 recommendations; four ways of assessing listed; proxy-task validity 'yet to be established'.
quote: while CT skills themselves transcend specific subjects or disciplines, exercising them successfully in certain contexts demands domain-specific knowledge
limits: Stated as of 1990.
agent_relevance: Warns that proxy tests may not measure CT; supports real task outcomes plus code checks as measures.

source: Ennis (1987) A taxonomy of critical thinking dispositions and abilities
finding: Not opened. From memory: Ennis defined CT as reasonable reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do, with a taxonomy of dispositions and abilities. SEP only lists the 1987 work and quotes the 1991 revision.
numbers: SEP gives the 1991 disposition: 'to determine and maintain focus on the conclusion or question'. No other numbers verified.
limits: Original not opened. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Defining CT as deciding what to believe or do fits what an agent does when it commits to an answer.

source: McPeck (1981) Critical thinking and education, as summarised in SEP
finding: McPeck argued CT abilities are subject-specific, so teaching thinking as a separate subject is futile. Paul and Siegel (1985) gave counterexamples from writing and speaking. Ennis (1989) called the weaker version vague.
numbers: SEP calls evidence for transfer across domains 'scanty'. No effect sizes given.
quote: it is a conceptual truth that all critical thinking abilities are specific to a subject
limits: Conceptual argument, not an experiment; second-hand through SEP.
agent_relevance: Supports domain-specific checkers (code tests, executors) rather than a generic 'think critically' prompt.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Paul, Lipman, Siegel, Bailin, Stanovich
finding: Competing ideals: Paul wants strong-sense CT (open to rival world views); Lipman wants criteria-based, context-sensitive, self-correcting thinking; Siegel grounds it in respect for persons and responsiveness to reasons; Bailin sees careful goal-directed thinking meeting standards; Stanovich adds overriding the autonomous mind.
numbers: Siegel names 4 considerations (respect for persons, self-sufficiency, initiation into rational traditions, democratic preparation).
quote: sensitive to context, relies on criteria, and is self-correcting
limits: Normative positions, not tested.
agent_relevance: All share a core: goal-directed, criterion-based, self-correcting. That core is what our scaffold can implement.

source: SEP: coverage of standard CT tests
finding: The tests cover only parts of the construct. Inference is 2 of 5 Watson-Glaser subtests, 11 of 34 California Critical Thinking Skills Test items, and 2 of 4 sections of Cornell Level X.
numbers: Cornell X: 76 items, 24 on credibility; Cornell Z: 52 items; CCTST 11/34 inference, 5/34 argument analysis; CLA 25 selected-response items.
limits: Counts as given in the entry.
agent_relevance: LLM scores on these tests cover a narrow slice and may be gamed by pattern matching.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically (as cited in SEP)
finding: Dialogue, anchored instruction and mentoring each raised effectiveness, best in combination. Separate CT instruction plus subject teaching beat either alone but not significantly.
numbers: No effect sizes in the visible SEP text; the paper itself was not opened (publisher page blocked).
limits: Numbers not verified. SEP says transfer evidence is scanty.
agent_relevance: Human teaching effects do not carry to agents; included for the founding claim that CT is partly teachable.

source: Critique Ability of Large Language Models (CriticBench), arXiv 2310.04815
finding: The paper treats critical thinking as the ability to critique answers and calls it overlooked in LLM evaluation. Critique is hard, emerging only in large models. Self-critique is harder. Critique accuracy tracks model certainty.
numbers: PaLM-2-L scored 54.14% on Critic-HumanEval, barely above chance. Medium and smaller models on GSM8K and TruthfulQA critique were near random.
limits: Final-judgement accuracy used as proxy for quality of analysis. 2023 models. Binary judge task.
agent_relevance: If self-critique is near chance, the scaffold must use external checks instead of self-review.

source: CriticBench: self-consistency with self-check on GSM8K (arXiv 2310.04815, Table 1)
finding: Using critique to filter votes only when certainty is low improves self-consistency a little. Error reduction was 3.03% (ChatGPT), 16.09% (PaLM-2) and 9.52% (GPT-4).
numbers: GSM8K SC@64 to SC with self-check: ChatGPT 83.5 to 84.0; PaLM-2 91.3 to 92.7; GPT-4 95.8 to 96.2.
limits: Gains are small in points; certainty threshold C=2 for GPT-4, C=1 for the others.
agent_relevance: Uncertainty-gated critique is cheap and slightly useful; supports gating extra checks on low agreement.

source: Can OpenAI o1 outperform humans in higher-order cognitive thinking? arXiv 2412.05753
finding: o1-preview was compared with published human data on the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test and other tests. It beat undergraduates and postgraduates on the essay test but scored worst on problem solving.
numbers: EWCTET 24.33 (runs of 20, 26, 27 of 29) vs undergraduates 13.8 and 11.51 (SD 8.23) and postgraduates 18.39 (SD 6.59); z 1.60 and 0.90. Problem solving: o1 1.00 vs human 3.68, z -4.25.
limits: Human data from separate studies, not parallel; role prompts not used with humans; z formula unstated and some do not recompute; text-only input.
agent_relevance: LLMs clear human averages on rubric-scored CT essays, so such tests do not separate agent designs. Need harder, executable checks.

source: o1 vs humans: other structured tests (arXiv 2412.05753)
finding: o1-preview scored above students on logic and systematic-thinking tasks and was near human level on a computational thinking scale.
numbers: Lake Urmia Vignette 46.10 (SD 4.12) vs 20.08 (SD 8.13), N=155, z 3.20; LogiQA 90% vs 86% (N=651); CT skills scale 3.84 vs 3.92, z -0.15; TOSLS 0.99 vs 0.85 top human.
limits: Comparison with published human means, 5 to 10 trials only.
agent_relevance: Where structure is clear, LLMs are at or above student level; ceiling effect for agent evaluation.

source: When All Options Are Wrong: incorrect multiple-choice options, arXiv 2409.00113
finding: The paper cites Dewey and tests whether LLMs notice that no multiple-choice option is correct. Instruction-tuned models mostly pick a wrong option anyway.
numbers: Basic Addition, no correct option, standard: Claude 3 Opus 8.65%, GPT-4o 6.71%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 14.02%, Llama-3.1-405B 54.72%, Gemini Flash 0.00%. Baseline with one correct option: 91.39, 82.19, 100.00, 79.63, 59.68. Human sample N=50 spotted 2.02 of 3 trick questions; 14 spotted none.
quote: Active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge
limits: Only addition and a 400-question MMLU subset; temperature 0; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: A concrete test of not following a faulty premise. Add an explicit none-of-the-above or premise-check state.

source: When All Options Are Wrong: alignment effect (arXiv 2409.00113)
finding: Instruction tuning made models worse at spotting invalid questions. The base Qwen2-Math-7B scored far above its Instruct version when all options were wrong.
numbers: Qwen2-Math-7B 0.965 vs Qwen2-Math-7B-Instruct 0.08; Llama-3.1-8B 0.00 in all three wrong-option variants.
limits: One model pair; the base model may refuse rather than reason.
agent_relevance: Instruction-following pressure suppresses premise checking; the scaffold must give explicit permission to reject the task.

source: Faulty Premises Bench (FPBench), arXiv 2508.03622
finding: Fifteen LLMs rarely notice faulty premises in code tasks unless told to look. Proactive recognition is low; prompted recognition is high.
numbers: PRER (no prompt): DeepSeek-R1 0.57 highest, O4-mini 0.12 lowest. PAER (told to check): GPT-4.1 0.81, DeepSeek-R1 0.77, Qwen3-235B 0.72; GPT-4.1 0.23 to 0.81. R1 length 1,756 to 2,493 tokens (2,734 with guidance).
limits: HumanEval and MBPP+ only; perturbations made by GPT-4o, checked by 3 annotators on 300 samples; text and table disagree on one number (R1 PRER 0.43 vs 0.57).
agent_relevance: The program should force a premise-check step instead of hoping the model volunteers it; longer output is not a proxy for checking.

source: Argument reconstruction as supervision for critical thinking in LLMs, arXiv 2603.17432
finding: Training small models to reconstruct arguments (3,175 examples, Arguinas) improves most of seven critical-thinking tasks. CT is defined as thinking clearly and rationally about what to do or believe, in three stages: identify, reconstruct, evaluate.
numbers: Base models with Arguinas: LegalArg 4B 47.24 to 58.52, 8B 54.70 to 62.87; ReClor 4B 74.13 to 78.98; ArgRC 4B 86.54 to 90.77. Instruct models mixed: Qwen3-4B LegalArg 65.42 to 61.75; Qwen2.5-7B ArgsNovel 49.72 to 47.52.
limits: Gains clear on base models, mixed on instruct models; fallacious arguments excluded because they hurt; data built with Claude Sonnet 4.5; training, not scaffolding.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit reconstruct-the-argument operator before evaluating; the benefit is training-time and small on stronger models.

source: Lee et al. (2025) Impact of generative AI on critical thinking, CHI 2025 survey
finding: Survey of 319 knowledge workers (936 usable examples) using Bloom's six-level taxonomy as the definition of CT. Workers said GenAI lowered perceived critical-thinking effort, and more trust in AI went with less effort.
numbers: N=319, 936 examples; CT enacted in 59.29% of examples; much less or less effort: knowledge 72%, comprehension 79%, application 69%, analysis 72%, synthesis 76%, evaluation 55%; trust in GenAI vs effort beta -0.12 (p=.029) knowledge, -0.17 (p=.002) application, -0.12 (p=.046) analysis, -0.24 (p<.001) evaluation.
limits: Self-report, Prolific sample, no causation, English only; effort may be conflated with cognitive effort in general. Bloom's taxonomy was chosen for simplicity and is contested.
agent_relevance: Human-side risk: a scaffold that hides its checks may lower the user's own checking. Output should invite verification.

source: Your Brain on ChatGPT, arXiv 2506.08872
finding: Essay writing with an LLM, a search engine or no tool over three sessions. LLM users had weakest brain connectivity (EEG), lowest ownership and poor quoting of their own essays, over four months.
numbers: 54 completed sessions 1-3; 18 completed session 4 (crossover LLM-to-brain, brain-to-LLM).
limits: Abstract page only read; small sample and heavy attrition.
agent_relevance: About human learning, not the agent; background on why the CT definition matters in AI-use studies.

source: Investigating LLM use on critical thinking under time constraints, arXiv 2603.08849
finding: 393-person experiment: early or continuous LLM access helped under time pressure but hurt when time was sufficient; starting independently showed the opposite.
numbers: N=393; 4 timing conditions (early, continuous, late, none) by 2 time conditions.
limits: Abstract page only; no effect sizes seen.
agent_relevance: Suggests when to hand off to the model: use it for speed under tight budget, not as first move when budget is generous.

source: Not Too Short, Not Too Long: LLM response length and critical thinking, arXiv 2603.06878
finding: 24 adults judged whether GPT-5 answers to 15 Watson-Glaser-style items were correct. Medium-length explanations helped them catch wrong conclusions.
numbers: Probability correct when LLM wrong: short 0.245, medium 0.542, long 0.307; when LLM right: 0.715, 0.811, 0.795.
limits: N=24; 15 of 40 original items; no no-AI baseline; length confounded with reading time; one model; no p-values in text.
agent_relevance: Human error detection on wrong LLM answers is only about 25-54%, so human review is a weak backstop; use code checks.

source: Toward LLM-supported automated assessment of critical thinking subskills, arXiv 2510.12915
finding: Scoring student argumentative essays on CT subskills: fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B did best among GPT-5, Llama 3.1 8B and ModernBERT; it did better on subskills with clear level separation and balanced labels.
numbers: Three models by three methods (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuning). No agreement figures on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only; no kappa or sample size seen.
agent_relevance: LLM scoring of CT works only on well-defined rubrics; ambiguous levels reduce reliability.

source: ELLIS Alicante at CQs-Gen 2025, arXiv 2506.14371
finding: Two small open models, a Questioner and a Judge, generate and select critical questions against weak claims and ranked first in the CQs-Gen shared task at the ACL 2025 argument mining workshop.
numbers: Rank 1; no score on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; shared-task metric not read.
agent_relevance: Generate-then-judge critical questions is an operator pattern we can reuse, with the judge run as a separate pass.
